checks.name: Determinant integral identity
hypotheses: The integer endpoint exponents are nonnegative, so every moment and derivative under the integral is dominated on bounded parameter intervals.

argument: The derivative of order k at zero is the kth moment. Expand the determinant of its moment matrix as a signed permutation sum, and put its products under the multiple integral.

checks.name: Sharp Landau inequality and mollified equality sequence
hypotheses: The function is real and twice continuously differentiable on the whole real line; both uniform bounds hold globally.
argument: For every t>0, subtract Taylor expansions at x+t and x-t. The difference of endpoint values is at most2M; the sum of remainder bounds is Nt^2. Hence |f prime(x)|<=M/t+Nt/2.

Optimize t=sqrt(2M/N). To show sharpness, take the periodic C1 perfect spline whose derivative is a triangle wave of height sqrt(2MN) and slope magnitude N, and whose function values oscillate between -M and M.

Convolve this periodic spline with nonnegative smooth probability mollifiers. Function amplitude remains at most M, the second derivative is at most N because the spline has an essentially bounded weak second derivative, and the derivative peak converges to sqrt(2MN). Thus the requested supremum is exact.

checks.name: Power-spaced infinite-product cutoff
hypotheses: The base exceeds one, the integer power is at least two, and the positive parameter decreases to zero.
argument: For each fixed t the logarithms converge absolutely in the tail, hence the product is positive. Set L=ln(1/t) and J=floor((L/ln b)^(1/p)).

For k<=J the argument u=t*b^(k^p) is at most one, and ln(1-exp(-u))=ln u+O(u) uniformly. Since adjacent k^p differ by at least one, the sum of these errors is bounded by a geometric series independent of t.
For k>J, the first argument exceeds one and subsequent arguments grow at least geometrically. The tail sum of logarithms is uniformly bounded.
Thus ln P=-(J+1)L+ln b*sum(k^p)+O(1). The power sum equals J^(p+1)/(p+1)+O(J^p), and J=(L/ln b)^(1/p)+O(1). Dividing by L^(1+1/p) gives the stated constant.

checks.name: Power-spaced infinite-product cutoff
hypotheses: The base exceeds one, the integer power is at least two, and the positive parameter decreases to zero.
argument: For each fixed t the logarithms converge absolutely in the tail, hence the product is positive. Set L=ln(1/t) and J=floor((L/ln b)^(1/p)).

For k<=J the argument u=t*b^(k^p) is at most one, and ln(1-exp(-u))=ln u+O(u) uniformly. Since adjacent k^p differ by at least one, the sum of these errors is bounded by a geometric series independent of t.
For k>J, the first argument exceeds one and subsequent arguments grow at least geometrically. The tail sum of logarithms is uniformly bounded.
Thus ln P=-(J+1)L+ln b*sum(k^p)+O(1). The power sum equals J^(p+1)/(p+1)+O(J^p), and J=(L/ln b)^(1/p)+O(1). Dividing by L^(1+1/p) gives the stated constant.

checks.name: Sharp concentration asymptotic
hypotheses: Functions are nonnegative on[0,1], Lipschitz constant at most n, and the pth-power integral is at most1/n.
In the zero-endpoint case both endpoint values vanish. In the free case there is no endpoint restriction.
argument: At a height M, the slope bound forces f(x)>=max(M-n|x-x0|,0). With zero endpoints the entire two-sided cone fits in[0,1], giving mass at least2M^(p+1)/(n(p+1)).

For free endpoints, if M/n<=1 the truncated cone has minimum integral when its peak lies at an endpoint, giving M^(p+1)/(n(p+1)). If M/n>1, an interval of length1/2 has height at least M-n/2, contradicting the vanishing mass budget for all sufficiently large n.

Thus the displayed constant bounds every peak for large n. A centered tent with zero endpoints, or an endpoint tent in the free case, has that height, slope n, and exactly mass1/n for all sufficiently large n.

hypotheses: Functions are nonnegative on[0,1], Lipschitz constant at most n, and the pth-power integral is at most1/n.
In the zero-endpoint case both endpoint values vanish. In the free case there is no endpoint restriction.
argument: At a height M, the slope bound forces f(x)>=max(M-n|x-x0|,0). With zero endpoints the entire two-sided cone fits in[0,1], giving mass at least2M^(p+1)/(n(p+1)).

checks.name: Exact discrete mixed-boundary spectrum
hypotheses: The optimizing vector is any nonzero real vector, and the number of coordinates tends to infinity along the displayed affine integer sequence.
argument: Let y_j be cumulative sums and y_0=0. The denominator becomes sum(y_j-y_(j-1))^2. Its symmetric matrix has diagonal2 except its final entry1, and adjacent entries-1.
The sine eigenvector y_j=sin(j theta) obeys the left boundary automatically. The last row is equivalent to sin((N+1)theta)=sin(N theta), so theta_l=(2l-1)pi/(2N+1), l=1..N.
These N distinct eigenvalues are2-2cos(theta_l)>0. The smallest is4sin^2(pi/(4N+2)); reciprocal gives the maximum Rayleigh quotient.
With N=an+b, divide by n^2 and use sin u/u->1.

hypotheses: For each fixed positive phase, the evaluation point lies in(-1,1) for all sufficiently large n.
Taylor remainders are uniform in a fixed neighborhood of the limiting angle.
argument: The recurrence gives P_n(cos theta)=cos(2^n theta) by induction. Differentiate to obtain P_n prime(cos theta)=2^n sin(2^n theta)/sin theta.

Divide these two expansions, subtract sin(alpha)/alpha, and multiply by N squared. The nonzero denominator alpha justifies the division and the remainder tends to zero.

checks.name: Rootwise gap identity
hypotheses: The monic polynomial is explicitly defined by its degree and differential equation. It has simple complex roots; no root approximation is used.
argument: Write P(x)=(x-r)Q(x) at a simple root. Then P second/(2P prime)=sum over other roots1/(r-s), and P third/(3P prime) is the square of that sum minus the sum of inverse squared gaps.
The ODE at r gives the first sum r. Differentiating the ODE once gives P third/P prime=4r^2-2(N-1). Consequently each inverse-square gap sum is[2(N-1)-r^2]/3.
Multiply by r^(2q) and sum over roots. Each unordered pair contributes exactly the displayed symmetric numerator. The required polynomial moments follow from Newton sums or companion-matrix traces.

choices.misconception: Count the two composed endpoint singularities as two inverse transforms
correct
Treat the Abel power coefficient as the density coefficient
Return the recovered density instead of its derivative

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Compose the given Abel transform with itself. Boundedness of the continuous density and integrability of both endpoint kernels justify absolute Fubini.}
f(x)=\frac1\pi\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\int_0^x\frac{F(t)}{\sqrt{x-t}}\,\mathrm dt,\qquad F(x)=- \frac{16 x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{15} + \frac{8 x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} + 2 \sqrt{x}

checks.name: Abel inversion with continuous density
hypotheses: The density is real continuous on the closed unit interval, hence bounded.
Both square-root endpoint singularities are integrable.
argument: Apply the same transform again. Absolute Fubini is justified by the bound on the density and the finite positive double-kernel integral.

case.purpose: Coprime even/odd frequencies give distinct dimensionless spectral ratios.

statement: \textnormal{Let f be a real twice continuously differentiable function of period }2\pi\textnormal{ satisfying }f^{\prime\prime}(x)+\frac{5}{2}f(x)=- \frac{3}{2}f(x+\pi),\qquad\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)^2\,\mathrm dx=\pi.\textnormal{Find the largest possible value of }|f\prime(0)|.

choices.misconception: Omit the factor pi in real trigonometric orthogonality
Count both signs of the odd Fourier mode as independent sine coefficients
correct
Count both signs of the even Fourier mode as independent sine coefficients

solutionSteps: \textnormal{A Fourier mode of index k receives the following factor. Integration by parts is valid because the function and its derivative are periodic.}
\textnormal{Fourier uniqueness therefore leaves only these two frequencies.}
f(x)=a \cos{\left(2 x \right)} + b \sin{\left(2 x \right)} + c \cos{\left(x \right)} + d \sin{\left(x \right)}
f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{5} \left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + 2 \sin{\left(2 x \right)}\right)}{5}\textnormal{ attains equality and satisfies the stated equation and normalization.}

checks.name: Complete Fourier exclusion and extremality
hypotheses: The real function is C2 and2pi-periodic. Its shifted second-order equation can be bootstrapped to all derivative orders.
argument: Integrate the equation against each exponential Fourier mode twice by parts; periodic boundary terms vanish. The shift multiplies mode k by(-1)^k.

The coefficient factor is e^2-k^2 for even k and o^2-k^2 for odd k, so only the four signed frequencies survive. Fourier uniqueness for continuous periodic functions identifies the function with that finite trigonometric sum.

Orthogonality converts the given integral to the squared Euclidean coefficient norm. The derivative is a linear functional of the two sine coefficients, whose norm is sqrt(e^2+o^2). The displayed function attains it.

statement: \textnormal{Let f be a real twice continuously differentiable function of period }2\pi\textnormal{ satisfying }f^{\prime\prime}(x)+\frac{17}{2}f(x)=- \frac{15}{2}f(x+\pi),\qquad\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)^2\,\mathrm dx=\pi.\textnormal{Find the largest possible value of }|f\prime(0)|.

choices.misconception: correct
Omit the factor pi in real trigonometric orthogonality
Count both signs of the even Fourier mode as independent sine coefficients
Count both signs of the odd Fourier mode as independent sine coefficients

solutionSteps: \textnormal{A Fourier mode of index k receives the following factor. Integration by parts is valid because the function and its derivative are periodic.}
\textnormal{Fourier uniqueness therefore leaves only these two frequencies.}
f(x)=a \cos{\left(4 x \right)} + b \sin{\left(4 x \right)} + c \cos{\left(x \right)} + d \sin{\left(x \right)}
f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{17} \left(\sin{\left(x \right)} + 4 \sin{\left(4 x \right)}\right)}{17}\textnormal{ attains equality and satisfies the stated equation and normalization.}

checks.name: Complete Fourier exclusion and extremality
hypotheses: The real function is C2 and2pi-periodic. Its shifted second-order equation can be bootstrapped to all derivative orders.
argument: Integrate the equation against each exponential Fourier mode twice by parts; periodic boundary terms vanish. The shift multiplies mode k by(-1)^k.

The coefficient factor is e^2-k^2 for even k and o^2-k^2 for odd k, so only the four signed frequencies survive. Fourier uniqueness for continuous periodic functions identifies the function with that finite trigonometric sum.

Orthogonality converts the given integral to the squared Euclidean coefficient norm. The derivative is a linear functional of the two sine coefficients, whose norm is sqrt(e^2+o^2). The displayed function attains it.

hypotheses: The real function is C2 and2pi-periodic. Its shifted second-order equation can be bootstrapped to all derivative orders.

K(t)=0\textnormal{ in the middle interval at }t=\frac{1}{6},\ \frac{5}{6}

hypotheses: The function is real and twice continuously differentiable on[0,1], with second derivative bounded by one.

case.purpose: Different tangent configurations and nonlinear perturbation directions.

statement: x^{4} + x^{3} y + 6 x^{3} - 5 x^{2} y + x y^{3} - 2 x y^{2} + y^{3}=0.\textnormal{Let the real analytic branches through the origin be }y_1(x),y_2(x),y_3(x).\textnormal{Find }\sum_{j=1}^3(y_j^{\prime\prime}(0))^2.

choices.misconception: Replace the sum of squares by the square of the sum
correct
Sum derivative magnitudes instead of their squares
Double the second derivative again before squaring

solutionSteps: \textnormal{At the origin the usual implicit derivative divides by zero. Resolve the tangent directions first.}
\textnormal{Each tangent root is simple, so the analytic implicit-function theorem gives precisely one resolved branch for each root.}

pedagogy.difficultyRationale: Ordinary implicit differentiation fails at the singular origin. Dividing after a tangent blowup separates the branches and reveals which derivative is actually determined.
pedagogy.nearestNeighborDistinction: The moving-root trace family starts with simple roots and sums them; this first resolves a singular plane curve with several distinct tangent directions.

checks.name: Resolve the singular point before differentiating
hypotheses: Only real analytic branches through the origin are requested, and the three displayed tangent roots are distinct and real.
argument: Substitute y=xu for x not zero and cancel x^3. The resolved equation is P(u)+xQ(u)=0. Each simple real root r of P gives one analytic u branch with u(0)=r.
Conversely every analytic branch y through zero has a finite initial slope and hence one of these roots; there are exactly three.
Differentiate the resolved equation at zero to obtain u prime(0)=-Q(r)/P prime(r). Since y=xu, y second(0)=2u prime(0). Square and sum the three values.

checks.name: Convex box-slice moment extremum
hypotheses: The polynomial is real of exactly the displayed degree, normalized to value one at zero; all roots lie in the displayed negative closed interval, with multiplicities allowed.
argument: Write p(x)=product(1+u_j x), where each positive u_j lies between the reciprocal bounds. The first derivative fixes sum u_j=S, and the second equals S^2-sum u_j^2.

If two coordinates are interior to their bounds, shift an amount from the smaller one to the larger while preserving their sum; their square sum cannot decrease. Continue until at most one coordinate is interior.

Thus the maximum square sum is achieved with the displayed number at the upper bound, the remaining endpoints at the lower bound, and one residual coordinate. The constructed polynomial verifies attainment.

case.purpose: Distinct absolute-distance moments; the irrational orbit itself is fixed to avoid fake parameter novelty.

statement: \{x\}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor.\textnormal{Evaluate }\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\left|\{n\sqrt2\}-\{n^2\sqrt2\}\right|^{1}.

choices.misconception: correct
Decrease the distance power by one in both integrations
Treat the distance as uniform on the unit interval
Multiply the coordinate moments instead of integrating their distance

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Test joint equidistribution with an arbitrary nonzero integer Fourier character.}
\textnormal{When the quadratic coefficient vanishes this is a geometric sum with nonunit ratio. Otherwise every fixed-lag correlation has the linear phase below.}

\textnormal{Its mean tends to zero because its slope is irrational. Van der Corput gives squared limsup at most one over an arbitrary window length; letting that length grow proves every nontrivial character has zero mean.}
\textnormal{Weyl criterion now applies jointly; arithmetic dependence has been checked rather than treated as independence.}

pedagogy.difficultyRationale: Two deterministic fractional-part coordinates must be shown jointly uniform despite their arithmetic dependence. Differencing quadratic phases reduces every nontrivial Fourier character to a controlled geometric sum.
pedagogy.nearestNeighborDistinction: The earlier irrational-rotation family concerns a linear orbit and a fixed phase correlation. Here the second coordinate is quadratic and the essential new step is differencing, not assuming independence.

checks.left: 2 \sqrt{2} N b h + \sqrt{2} a h + \sqrt{2} b h^{2}
checks.right: 2 \sqrt{2} N b h + \sqrt{2} \left(a h + b h^{2}\right)

checks.description: Independent triangle integration gives the limiting moment

checks.name: Joint polynomial equidistribution
hypotheses: The fixed irrational coefficient is square root two. Fourier character indices are integers, not both zero. The distance power is a positive integer.
argument: For a nonzero character(a,b), the exponential phase is square-root-two times(a*n+b*n squared). If b=0, the average is a geometric sum with ratio different from one and tends to zero.
If b is nonzero, every fixed positive-lag correlation has a linear phase with nonzero irrational slope2*b*h*sqrt2, so it also tends to zero by the same geometric-sum estimate.
The van der Corput inequality, with a fixed correlation window H and then the sample size tending to infinity, bounds the squared limsup of the original average by1/H. Let H tend to infinity.

Weyl criterion therefore gives joint uniformity on the square. The fractional-coordinate distance power is bounded and has discontinuities only on the boundary identifications, a null set, so Riemann-integrable equidistribution applies.
Split the square along the diagonal and integrate twice the lower triangle to obtain the exact moment.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{Test joint equidistribution with an arbitrary nonzero integer Fourier character.}
\textnormal{When the quadratic coefficient vanishes this is a geometric sum with nonunit ratio. Otherwise every fixed-lag correlation has the linear phase below.}

\textnormal{Its mean tends to zero because its slope is irrational. Van der Corput gives squared limsup at most one over an arbitrary window length; letting that length grow proves every nontrivial character has zero mean.}
\textnormal{Weyl criterion now applies jointly; arithmetic dependence has been checked rather than treated as independence.}

checks.description: Independent triangle integration gives the limiting moment

checks.name: Joint polynomial equidistribution
hypotheses: The fixed irrational coefficient is square root two. Fourier character indices are integers, not both zero. The distance power is a positive integer.
argument: For a nonzero character(a,b), the exponential phase is square-root-two times(a*n+b*n squared). If b=0, the average is a geometric sum with ratio different from one and tends to zero.
If b is nonzero, every fixed positive-lag correlation has a linear phase with nonzero irrational slope2*b*h*sqrt2, so it also tends to zero by the same geometric-sum estimate.
The van der Corput inequality, with a fixed correlation window H and then the sample size tending to infinity, bounds the squared limsup of the original average by1/H. Let H tend to infinity.

Weyl criterion therefore gives joint uniformity on the square. The fractional-coordinate distance power is bounded and has discontinuities only on the boundary identifications, a null set, so Riemann-integrable equidistribution applies.
Split the square along the diagonal and integrate twice the lower triangle to obtain the exact moment.

statement: P(t)=\prod_{k=1}^\infty(1-e^{-kt})^{k^{\frac{1}{2}}}\quad(t>0).\textnormal{Real powers are defined using the natural logarithm. Use }\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty u^{a-1}e^{-u}\,\mathrm du\ (a>0),\qquad\zeta(s)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty j^{-s}\ (s>1).\textnormal{Find }\lim_{t\downarrow0}t^{\frac{3}{2}}\ln P(t).

choices.misconception: correct
Insert the logarithmic expansion factor twice
Apply the logarithmic expansion divisor three times
Retain only the first logarithmic expansion term

solutionSteps: \textnormal{All terms are nonnegative, so the double sum is justified by Tonelli. For each fixed outer index, use a scaled Riemann sum.}

\textnormal{The normalized inner sums are bounded by a constant times the indicated inverse power of j, uniformly in the small parameter. Integral comparison handles small scaled j times t; exponential decay handles large scaled values.}
\textnormal{The dominating series converges. Pass the limit through the outer sum and restore the logarithm sign.}

checks.name: Uniform double-series singular limit
hypotheses: The product is defined by its convergent real logarithmic sum for every positive t; each base factor is in(0,1).
The power p is the stated positive rational number.
argument: Expand minus ln(1-exp(-kt)) as sum over j of exp(-jkt)/j. All terms are nonnegative, so Tonelli permits the double sum before any limiting step.
For each fixed j, t^(p+1)sum k^p exp(-jkt) is a Riemann sum tending to Gamma(p+1)/j^(p+1). The infinite tail is controlled by exponential decay.

Uniformly for v>0, v^(p+1)sum k^p exp(-vk) is bounded by a finite constant depending only on p. For v<=1 compare with the integral of(x+1)^p exp(-vx). For v>=1 use exp(-vk)<=exp(-v/2)exp(-k/2), whose polynomially weighted series converges.
With v=jt, the outer summand after normalization is bounded by C_p/j^(p+2). Dominated convergence for the j series therefore gives Gamma(p+1)zeta(p+2), with a negative sign for the product logarithm.

checks.name: Uniform double-series singular limit
hypotheses: The product is defined by its convergent real logarithmic sum for every positive t; each base factor is in(0,1).
The power p is the stated positive rational number.
argument: Expand minus ln(1-exp(-kt)) as sum over j of exp(-jkt)/j. All terms are nonnegative, so Tonelli permits the double sum before any limiting step.
For each fixed j, t^(p+1)sum k^p exp(-jkt) is a Riemann sum tending to Gamma(p+1)/j^(p+1). The infinite tail is controlled by exponential decay.

Uniformly for v>0, v^(p+1)sum k^p exp(-vk) is bounded by a finite constant depending only on p. For v<=1 compare with the integral of(x+1)^p exp(-vx). For v>=1 use exp(-vk)<=exp(-v/2)exp(-k/2), whose polynomially weighted series converges.
With v=jt, the outer summand after normalization is bounded by C_p/j^(p+2). Dominated convergence for the j series therefore gives Gamma(p+1)zeta(p+2), with a negative sign for the product logarithm.

statement: \textnormal{Independently place n balls into n boxes, each ball choosing every box with equal probability. Let }M_n\textnormal{ be the largest number of balls in any box. Find the constant c for which, for every positive delta, }\Pr\!\left(\left|\frac{M_n\ln\ln n}{\ln n}-c\right|<\delta\right)\longrightarrow1\quad(n\to\infty).

choices.misconception: correct
Apply the two-sided threshold margin twice
Double the threshold from a two-sided tail bound
Replace the largest load by the bounded average load

solutionSteps: k_+=(1+\varepsilon)\frac{\ln n}{\ln\ln n},\qquad\Pr(M_n\ge\lceil k_+\rceil)\le\frac n{\lceil k_+\rceil!}\longrightarrow0
\textnormal{For the lower bound, temporarily make the box counts independent Poisson variables with mean one.}
\textnormal{Conditioning the independent Poisson counts on their sum being n gives exactly the original box counts. The conditioning event has only a polynomially small probability.}
\textnormal{The lower-tail failure remains negligible after division by this probability. Combining the two bounds and letting the fixed tolerance vary proves the claimed constant.}

pedagogy.difficultyRationale: The maximum occupancy is governed by a threshold where a factorial tail balances the number of boxes. The lower bound needs a dependence argument; conditioning independent Poisson counts closes it with a quantified error.
pedagogy.nearestNeighborDistinction: The coupon collector asks when every box is nonempty. Here the extreme upper occupancy grows logarithmically, and Poissonization is used to prove a lower bound that a union bound cannot supply.

checks.name: Maximum occupancy logarithmic threshold
hypotheses: Exactly n independent balls choose uniformly among exactly n boxes. The maximum load is the number of balls in the fullest box.
argument: For k=(1+epsilon)ln n/ln ln n, the binomial factorial-moment bound gives P(M_n>=k)<=n/k!; Stirling makes its logarithm at most minus epsilon ln n plus lower-order terms.
For the lower bound use independent Poisson-one counts Y_1,...,Y_n. For k=(1-epsilon)ln n/ln ln n, P(Y_i>=k)>=e^-1/k!=n^(-1+epsilon+o1), so P(max Y_i<k)<=exp(-n^(epsilon+o1)).

Conditioned on sum Y_i=n, the counts have exactly the original multinomial occupancy law. Stirling gives P(sum Y_i=n) asymptotic to1/sqrt(2pi n). Dividing the exponentially small failure probability by this conditioning probability still gives zero.
Combining upper and lower estimates for every fixed positive epsilon proves the stated convergence in probability. Floor and ceiling of the threshold affect only lower-order terms.

checks.name: Full-circle saddle with exact prefactor
hypotheses: The positive quadratic exponential coefficient and critical point are the displayed finite rational values. The analytic implicit solution exists uniquely near zero by the implicit-function theorem.
argument: Lagrange inversion gives a_n=(1/n)[u^(n-1)]exp(n(u+cu squared)). Integrate on the circle u=tau exp(i theta).
After extracting rho^(-n), the remaining prefactor is tau/n and the integral is exp(n Phi(theta))exp(i theta), divided by2pi. Stationarity is tau+2c tau squared=1.
The real phase equals tau(cos theta-1)+c tau squared(cos2theta-1). Its unique maximum on[-pi,pi] is zero at theta0; outside every fixed neighborhood it is bounded above by a negative constant.

Near zero Phi(theta)=-variance*theta squared/2+O(theta cubed), with variance=tau+4c tau squared>0. Rescale theta=v/sqrt(n), dominate by a fixed Gaussian in a small neighborhood, and discard the exponentially small complement.
The local integral is asymptotic to sqrt(2pi/(n*variance)). Multiplying the coefficient prefactor gives tau/sqrt(2pi*variance), with the power n^(-3/2).

statement: \textnormal{Choose a permutation uniformly from all permutations of }\{1,2,\ldots,3n\}.\textnormal{Let }p_n\textnormal{ be the probability that every cycle has length divisible by }3\textnormal{. With }\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,\mathrm dt\quad(a>0),\textnormal{evaluate }\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{\frac{2}{3}}p_n.

choices.misconception: Count both orientations of each cycle as distinct
Divide the cycle weight by an extra orientation factor
correct
Apply the cycle-length factor twice

solutionSteps: \textnormal{A cycle of length k on labelled elements contributes one over k to the exponential generating function. Taking an unordered collection of allowed cycles exponentiates their contributions.}
\textnormal{Let }q_N\textnormal{ be the analogous probability on N labels, so }p_n=q_{3n}.\qquad\sum_{N\ge0}q_Nz^N=\exp\left(\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{z^{3j}}{3j}\right)=(1-z^{3})^{-\frac{1}{3}}
\textnormal{The ambient factorial has already canceled because these are probabilities, not counts. Stirling at two fixed shifts gives the ratio below.}

pedagogy.difficultyRationale: A probability over all permutations is converted into an exponential generating function by accounting for cyclic order and indistinguishable cycles. Its fractional singularity then determines the exact power-law constant.
pedagogy.nearestNeighborDistinction: The coupon collector counts missing labels; this problem constrains the complete cycle decomposition of a permutation and requires the cycle-index factor.

checks.name: Permutation cycle probability asymptotic
hypotheses: The permutation is uniform on the full symmetric group of size d*n; all cycles, including singleton cycles, are subject to the divisibility condition.
The Gamma function is defined for positive arguments.
argument: A labelled cycle of length k has(k-1)! arrangements, so its exponential generating contribution is z^k/k. Unordered collections of allowed cycles exponentiate their sum.
The probability generating series is exp(sum z^(dj)/(dj))=(1-z^d)^(-1/d). Therefore the desired probability is(1/d)_n/n!, with no extra factorial from the ambient size.
Write this coefficient as Gamma(n+1/d)/(Gamma(1/d)Gamma(n+1)). Stirling applied at the two shifted arguments gives the ratio n^(1/d-1)(1+o1).
The requested normalization uses n, not the total number d*n of labels.

checks.name: Last-zero distribution and endpoint control
hypotheses: The increments are independent and take the values plus/minus one with equal probability. The last zero includes time zero.
The observation fraction is strictly between zero and one.
argument: Let u_j=binomial(2j,j)/4^j. A reflection/ballot count gives probability u_m of no return to zero during the next2m steps after time zero. Independence at a specified last zero gives P(L_(2n)=2k)=u_k*u_(n-k).
Stirling gives u_k~1/sqrt(pi*k), and the central-binomial estimate u_k<=C/sqrt(k+1) holds uniformly, including k0.
On any fixed closed subinterval of(0,1), the last-zero probabilities give an ordinary Riemann sum for1/(pi sqrt(t(1-t))).
The sum of terms with k<=delta*n is at most C sqrt(delta)+O(n^(-1/2)); the same bound holds near the other endpoint. These estimates justify removing the truncation.
Integrate the density from zero to the stated fraction using t=sin squared(theta), obtaining2arcsin(sqrt(a))/pi.

hypotheses: All four moduli are positive integers, the leading and linear coefficients are the stated integers, and n tends through positive integers.
argument: If g=gcd(a,m) does not divide b, shifting by m/g gives a nontrivial geometric character and the sum vanishes. Otherwise split into g identical periods, obtaining g times the reduced sum with modulus m/g and coefficients a/g,b/g.

statement: \textnormal{An urn initially contains 1 red balls and 2 blue balls. On every draw, choose a ball uniformly, return it, and add one more ball of the same color. Let the red fraction after n draws be }X_n.\textnormal{Find }\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P(X_n>\frac{1}{2}).

choices.misconception: correct
Use the initial mean as a tail probability
Return the complementary lower-tail probability
Average the tail with one as though half the mass were an endpoint atom

solutionSteps: K_n=\textnormal{number of red draws},\qquad\mathbb P(K_n=k)=\binom nk\frac{(1)_k(2)_{n-k}}{(3)_n}
\textnormal{The ordered draw probability depends only on the number of red draws, not their order. This gives the displayed exchangeable count law.}

\textnormal{Factorial cancellation bounds the endpoint portions as well, so these masses converge by Riemann sums to the density below. The actual red fraction differs from the draw fraction by a quantity tending uniformly to zero.}

checks.name: Beta-binomial law and density limit
hypotheses: Initially there are the displayed positive integer counts of two colors. Each draw is uniform, the drawn ball is returned, and one additional ball of its color is added.
argument: Every ordered draw string with k red and n-k blue draws has the same probability: the product of red rising factors times blue rising factors divided by the total rising factors. Count the binomial number of such strings.
For positive integer initial counts, factorial cancellation gives a polynomial-in-k,n representation. Uniformly on compact subintervals of(0,1), n times the mass at k tends to the beta density.

The same explicit polynomial bounds control the endpoint mass by a constant times the endpoint interval length to the corresponding positive initial exponent. Thus Riemann sums converge on the full interval, and the continuous limiting density has no atom at the threshold.
The actual red fraction differs from k/n by O(1/n), so it has the same limiting tail probability.

hypotheses: Initially there are the displayed positive integer counts of two colors. Each draw is uniform, the drawn ball is returned, and one additional ball of its color is added.

checks.name: From the partition product to an exact coefficient
hypotheses: The exclusion modulus is an integer at least two, so part one is always allowed. Part multiplicities are unrestricted nonnegative integers. The infinite product converges at every positive real t.
argument: Let C(t)=sum over k>=1 of -ln(1-exp(-tk)). Its integrable logarithmic singularity at zero and exponentially small tail give t*C(t)->integral0infinity -ln(1-exp(-u))du=pi^2/6. The integral follows by the nonnegative log series and Tonelli. Thus lnZ(t)=C(t)-C(dt)~A/t, where A=(1-1/d)pi^2/6.
Since p(n)exp(-tn)<=Z(t), choose t=sqrt(A/n) to get limsup ln p(n)/sqrt n<=2sqrt(A).

For a lower bound take independent geometric counts X_k, for allowed k, with P(X_k=j)=(1-exp(-tk))*exp(-tkj). The total N=sum kX_k is finite almost surely because its expectation is finite, and P(N=m)=p(m)exp(-tm)/Z(t).

Independent Riemann-sum arguments, rather than differentiating an asymptotic equivalence, give EN~A/t^2 and VarN~2A/t^3. The needed integrals are integral u/(exp u-1)=pi^2/6 and integral u^2 exp u/(exp u-1)^2=pi^2/3; nonnegative geometric series justify their values.
For fixed0<epsilon<1/2 put t=sqrt(A/((1-epsilon)n)). Then EN~(1-epsilon)n and VarN=O(n^(3/2)). Chebyshev implies P((1-2epsilon)n<=N<=n)->1.

Adding ones injects partitions of any m<=n into partitions of n, so p(m)<=p(n). The probability identity on the window gives Z(t)P(window)<=(n+1)p(n)exp(-t(1-2epsilon)n). Take logarithms, divide bysqrt n, then let epsilon decrease to zero. This gives the matching liminf.

prerequisites: Riemann sums with integrable endpoint singularities

case.purpose: Different dimensionless forbidden-part densities; no external amplitude or index scaling.

statement: \textnormal{Let }p_{3}(n)\textnormal{ be the number of integer partitions of n using only positive parts not divisible by }3\textnormal{. The order of the parts does not matter. Find }\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln p_{3}(n)}{\sqrt n}.

choices.misconception: Normalize the allowed residue count by the next modulus
Square the modulus in the excluded frequency
correct
Shift the forbidden modulus twice

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The endpoint singularity is integrable and the tail is exponentially bounded. The nonnegative logarithmic series evaluates the integral term by term. Removing the forbidden multiples gives}
\textnormal{The reverse bound needs coefficient information. Give each allowed part size an independent geometric multiplicity and let N be the resulting total size.}
\textnormal{These follow from separate Riemann sums for the first and second geometric moments, so no derivative of an asymptotic formula is assumed.}

\textnormal{Chebyshev applies because the variance is of order n to the three-halves power, smaller than the squared window width. Adding parts of size one injects every partition at a smaller size into the target size.}
\textnormal{Take logarithms, divide by the square root of n, and let epsilon tend to zero. The lower bound matches the upper bound.}

checks.name: From the partition product to an exact coefficient
hypotheses: The exclusion modulus is an integer at least two, so part one is always allowed. Part multiplicities are unrestricted nonnegative integers. The infinite product converges at every positive real t.
argument: Let C(t)=sum over k>=1 of -ln(1-exp(-tk)). Its integrable logarithmic singularity at zero and exponentially small tail give t*C(t)->integral0infinity -ln(1-exp(-u))du=pi^2/6. The integral follows by the nonnegative log series and Tonelli. Thus lnZ(t)=C(t)-C(dt)~A/t, where A=(1-1/d)pi^2/6.
Since p(n)exp(-tn)<=Z(t), choose t=sqrt(A/n) to get limsup ln p(n)/sqrt n<=2sqrt(A).

For a lower bound take independent geometric counts X_k, for allowed k, with P(X_k=j)=(1-exp(-tk))*exp(-tkj). The total N=sum kX_k is finite almost surely because its expectation is finite, and P(N=m)=p(m)exp(-tm)/Z(t).

Independent Riemann-sum arguments, rather than differentiating an asymptotic equivalence, give EN~A/t^2 and VarN~2A/t^3. The needed integrals are integral u/(exp u-1)=pi^2/6 and integral u^2 exp u/(exp u-1)^2=pi^2/3; nonnegative geometric series justify their values.
For fixed0<epsilon<1/2 put t=sqrt(A/((1-epsilon)n)). Then EN~(1-epsilon)n and VarN=O(n^(3/2)). Chebyshev implies P((1-2epsilon)n<=N<=n)->1.

Adding ones injects partitions of any m<=n into partitions of n, so p(m)<=p(n). The probability identity on the window gives Z(t)P(window)<=(n+1)p(n)exp(-t(1-2epsilon)n). Take logarithms, divide bysqrt n, then let epsilon decrease to zero. This gives the matching liminf.

argument: Let C(t)=sum over k>=1 of -ln(1-exp(-tk)). Its integrable logarithmic singularity at zero and exponentially small tail give t*C(t)->integral0infinity -ln(1-exp(-u))du=pi^2/6. The integral follows by the nonnegative log series and Tonelli. Thus lnZ(t)=C(t)-C(dt)~A/t, where A=(1-1/d)pi^2/6.
Since p(n)exp(-tn)<=Z(t), choose t=sqrt(A/n) to get limsup ln p(n)/sqrt n<=2sqrt(A).

For a lower bound take independent geometric counts X_k, for allowed k, with P(X_k=j)=(1-exp(-tk))*exp(-tkj). The total N=sum kX_k is finite almost surely because its expectation is finite, and P(N=m)=p(m)exp(-tm)/Z(t).

Independent Riemann-sum arguments, rather than differentiating an asymptotic equivalence, give EN~A/t^2 and VarN~2A/t^3. The needed integrals are integral u/(exp u-1)=pi^2/6 and integral u^2 exp u/(exp u-1)^2=pi^2/3; nonnegative geometric series justify their values.
For fixed0<epsilon<1/2 put t=sqrt(A/((1-epsilon)n)). Then EN~(1-epsilon)n and VarN=O(n^(3/2)). Chebyshev implies P((1-2epsilon)n<=N<=n)->1.

Adding ones injects partitions of any m<=n into partitions of n, so p(m)<=p(n). The probability identity on the window gives Z(t)P(window)<=(n+1)p(n)exp(-t(1-2epsilon)n). Take logarithms, divide bysqrt n, then let epsilon decrease to zero. This gives the matching liminf.

statement: \textnormal{Let }p_{9}(n)\textnormal{ be the number of integer partitions of n using only positive parts not divisible by }9\textnormal{. The order of the parts does not matter. Find }\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln p_{9}(n)}{\sqrt n}.

choices.misconception: correct
Halve the allowed density
Normalize the allowed residue count by the next modulus
Keep one allowed residue rather than all allowed residues

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The endpoint singularity is integrable and the tail is exponentially bounded. The nonnegative logarithmic series evaluates the integral term by term. Removing the forbidden multiples gives}
\textnormal{The reverse bound needs coefficient information. Give each allowed part size an independent geometric multiplicity and let N be the resulting total size.}
\textnormal{These follow from separate Riemann sums for the first and second geometric moments, so no derivative of an asymptotic formula is assumed.}

\textnormal{Chebyshev applies because the variance is of order n to the three-halves power, smaller than the squared window width. Adding parts of size one injects every partition at a smaller size into the target size.}
\textnormal{Take logarithms, divide by the square root of n, and let epsilon tend to zero. The lower bound matches the upper bound.}

checks.name: From the partition product to an exact coefficient
hypotheses: The exclusion modulus is an integer at least two, so part one is always allowed. Part multiplicities are unrestricted nonnegative integers. The infinite product converges at every positive real t.
argument: Let C(t)=sum over k>=1 of -ln(1-exp(-tk)). Its integrable logarithmic singularity at zero and exponentially small tail give t*C(t)->integral0infinity -ln(1-exp(-u))du=pi^2/6. The integral follows by the nonnegative log series and Tonelli. Thus lnZ(t)=C(t)-C(dt)~A/t, where A=(1-1/d)pi^2/6.
Since p(n)exp(-tn)<=Z(t), choose t=sqrt(A/n) to get limsup ln p(n)/sqrt n<=2sqrt(A).

For a lower bound take independent geometric counts X_k, for allowed k, with P(X_k=j)=(1-exp(-tk))*exp(-tkj). The total N=sum kX_k is finite almost surely because its expectation is finite, and P(N=m)=p(m)exp(-tm)/Z(t).

Independent Riemann-sum arguments, rather than differentiating an asymptotic equivalence, give EN~A/t^2 and VarN~2A/t^3. The needed integrals are integral u/(exp u-1)=pi^2/6 and integral u^2 exp u/(exp u-1)^2=pi^2/3; nonnegative geometric series justify their values.
For fixed0<epsilon<1/2 put t=sqrt(A/((1-epsilon)n)). Then EN~(1-epsilon)n and VarN=O(n^(3/2)). Chebyshev implies P((1-2epsilon)n<=N<=n)->1.

Adding ones injects partitions of any m<=n into partitions of n, so p(m)<=p(n). The probability identity on the window gives Z(t)P(window)<=(n+1)p(n)exp(-t(1-2epsilon)n). Take logarithms, divide bysqrt n, then let epsilon decrease to zero. This gives the matching liminf.

statement: \textnormal{Let }p_{12}(n)\textnormal{ be the number of integer partitions of n using only positive parts not divisible by }12\textnormal{. The order of the parts does not matter. Find }\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\ln p_{12}(n)}{\sqrt n}.

choices.misconception: correct

Halve the allowed density
Normalize the allowed residue count by the next modulus

solutionSteps: \textnormal{The endpoint singularity is integrable and the tail is exponentially bounded. The nonnegative logarithmic series evaluates the integral term by term. Removing the forbidden multiples gives}
\textnormal{The reverse bound needs coefficient information. Give each allowed part size an independent geometric multiplicity and let N be the resulting total size.}
\textnormal{These follow from separate Riemann sums for the first and second geometric moments, so no derivative of an asymptotic formula is assumed.}

\textnormal{Chebyshev applies because the variance is of order n to the three-halves power, smaller than the squared window width. Adding parts of size one injects every partition at a smaller size into the target size.}
\textnormal{Take logarithms, divide by the square root of n, and let epsilon tend to zero. The lower bound matches the upper bound.}

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For the first identity use the increasing substitution below and evenness of the resulting whole-line integrand.}
\textnormal{For the second identity use the following decreasing substitution on the interval from zero to b. It maps onto the interval from A to infinity and contributes a factor one half.}
\textnormal{Arithmetic and geometric means converge to a common positive value, so the parameters tend to zero. For the complementary integral use its tangent-variable representation.}

\textnormal{Split the improper integral at one and at the inverse square root of m. The outer parts stay bounded. In the middle, subtract one over u; the error is bounded by a constant times the sum of inverse-cubic u and m times u, with bounded integral.}
\textnormal{To determine the requested prefactor, the bounded error in the logarithm is insufficient. Retain the exact endpoint constant using a symmetric cutoff.}

\textnormal{The inversion below preserves the integral and exchanges the two pieces at the cutoff. On the lower piece, replacing the second square root by one incurs an error of order the square root of m.}
\textnormal{The ordinary invariant also determines the positive common limit. Combine it with the exact coordinate-difference formula.}

checks.name: Exact logarithmic constant and normalized gap
hypotheses: The ordinary and complementary integral identities above hold on the positive branch. The parameter m tends to zero through positive values.
argument: In the tangent representation of K(1-m), the inversion t=1/(sqrt(m)*u) leaves the integral kernel invariant. Split at its fixed point T=m^(-1/4), obtaining exactly twice the integral from0toT.
On this interval replace(1+m*t squared)^(-1/2) by1. The absolute integrated error is bounded by C*m*integral0T t squared/sqrt(1+t squared)dt=O(sqrt(m)).
The remaining integral is2asinh(T)=ln4-(1/2)ln m+O(sqrt(m)). Together with K(m)=pi/2+O(m), this gives exp(-pi*K(1-m)/K(m))=(m/16)(1+o1).

Complementary doubling makes this exponential exactly q^(2^n) at iteration n. Hence m_n is asymptotic to16q^(2^n). The coordinate difference equals a_n*m_n/(1+sqrt(1-m_n)), so its normalized limit is8M, where M=pi/(2K(p)).

checks.name: Complementary integral doubling and the gap root
hypotheses: At every step a>b>0. The elliptic parameter is m=1-(b/a)^2, strictly between zero and one. All square roots use the positive real branch.
argument: Define I(a,b)=integral0infinity dt/sqrt((t^2+a^2)(t^2+b^2)) and J(a,b)=integral0b dt/sqrt((a^2-t^2)(b^2-t^2)). The substitutions t=b tan theta and t=b sin theta give I=K(m)/a and J=K(1-m)/a.
For I use u=(t-ab/t)/2. It is an increasing bijection onto the real line; the two factorizations and its Jacobian give I(a,b)=I((a+b)/2,sqrt(ab)), using evenness.

For J use u=(t+ab/t)/2 on0<t<b. This is decreasing from infinity to(a+b)/2; both square-root factors stay positive. It gives one half the integral from the arithmetic mean to infinity of[(u^2-A^2)(u^2-G^2)]^(-1/2). The inversion v=A*G/u converts that exterior integral exactly to J(A,G). Thus J(A,G)=2J(a,b).
Consequently R_n=K(1-m_n)/K(m_n) equals2^n R_0. The ordinary arithmetic/geometric inequalities show both coordinates tend to a common positive limit, so m_n tends to zero.

For small m, K(m)=pi/2+O(m). In K(1-m)=integral0infinity du/sqrt((1+u^2)(1+m u^2)), split at1 and1/sqrt(m). The first and last pieces are uniformly bounded. On the middle interval the difference from1/u is bounded by a constant times(u^-3+m*u), whose integral is uniformly bounded. Hence K(1-m)=-(1/2)ln m+O(1).
It follows that pi R_n=-ln m_n+O(1). Also a_n-b_n=a_n*m_n/(1+sqrt(1-m_n)), whose ratio to m_n stays between positive constants. Divide logarithms by2^n and exponentiate to get the stated nome.

solutionSteps: \textnormal{For the first identity use the increasing substitution below and evenness of the resulting whole-line integrand.}
\textnormal{For the second identity use the following decreasing substitution on the interval from zero to b. It maps onto the interval from A to infinity and contributes a factor one half.}
\textnormal{Arithmetic and geometric means converge to a common positive value, so the parameters tend to zero. For the complementary integral use its tangent-variable representation.}

\textnormal{Split the improper integral at one and at the inverse square root of m. The outer parts stay bounded. In the middle, subtract one over u; the error is bounded by a constant times the sum of inverse-cubic u and m times u, with bounded integral.}

checks.name: Exact logarithmic constant and normalized gap
hypotheses: The ordinary and complementary integral identities above hold on the positive branch. The parameter m tends to zero through positive values.
argument: In the tangent representation of K(1-m), the inversion t=1/(sqrt(m)*u) leaves the integral kernel invariant. Split at its fixed point T=m^(-1/4), obtaining exactly twice the integral from0toT.
On this interval replace(1+m*t squared)^(-1/2) by1. The absolute integrated error is bounded by C*m*integral0T t squared/sqrt(1+t squared)dt=O(sqrt(m)).
The remaining integral is2asinh(T)=ln4-(1/2)ln m+O(sqrt(m)). Together with K(m)=pi/2+O(m), this gives exp(-pi*K(1-m)/K(m))=(m/16)(1+o1).

Complementary doubling makes this exponential exactly q^(2^n) at iteration n. Hence m_n is asymptotic to16q^(2^n). The coordinate difference equals a_n*m_n/(1+sqrt(1-m_n)), so its normalized limit is8M, where M=pi/(2K(p)).

checks.name: Complementary integral doubling and the gap root
hypotheses: At every step a>b>0. The elliptic parameter is m=1-(b/a)^2, strictly between zero and one. All square roots use the positive real branch.
argument: Define I(a,b)=integral0infinity dt/sqrt((t^2+a^2)(t^2+b^2)) and J(a,b)=integral0b dt/sqrt((a^2-t^2)(b^2-t^2)). The substitutions t=b tan theta and t=b sin theta give I=K(m)/a and J=K(1-m)/a.
For I use u=(t-ab/t)/2. It is an increasing bijection onto the real line; the two factorizations and its Jacobian give I(a,b)=I((a+b)/2,sqrt(ab)), using evenness.

For J use u=(t+ab/t)/2 on0<t<b. This is decreasing from infinity to(a+b)/2; both square-root factors stay positive. It gives one half the integral from the arithmetic mean to infinity of[(u^2-A^2)(u^2-G^2)]^(-1/2). The inversion v=A*G/u converts that exterior integral exactly to J(A,G). Thus J(A,G)=2J(a,b).
Consequently R_n=K(1-m_n)/K(m_n) equals2^n R_0. The ordinary arithmetic/geometric inequalities show both coordinates tend to a common positive limit, so m_n tends to zero.

For small m, K(m)=pi/2+O(m). In K(1-m)=integral0infinity du/sqrt((1+u^2)(1+m u^2)), split at1 and1/sqrt(m). The first and last pieces are uniformly bounded. On the middle interval the difference from1/u is bounded by a constant times(u^-3+m*u), whose integral is uniformly bounded. Hence K(1-m)=-(1/2)ln m+O(1).
It follows that pi R_n=-ln m_n+O(1). Also a_n-b_n=a_n*m_n/(1+sqrt(1-m_n)), whose ratio to m_n stays between positive constants. Divide logarithms by2^n and exponentiate to get the stated nome.

argument: Define I(a,b)=integral0infinity dt/sqrt((t^2+a^2)(t^2+b^2)) and J(a,b)=integral0b dt/sqrt((a^2-t^2)(b^2-t^2)). The substitutions t=b tan theta and t=b sin theta give I=K(m)/a and J=K(1-m)/a.
For I use u=(t-ab/t)/2. It is an increasing bijection onto the real line; the two factorizations and its Jacobian give I(a,b)=I((a+b)/2,sqrt(ab)), using evenness.

For J use u=(t+ab/t)/2 on0<t<b. This is decreasing from infinity to(a+b)/2; both square-root factors stay positive. It gives one half the integral from the arithmetic mean to infinity of[(u^2-A^2)(u^2-G^2)]^(-1/2). The inversion v=A*G/u converts that exterior integral exactly to J(A,G). Thus J(A,G)=2J(a,b).

On the middle interval the difference from1/u is bounded by a constant times(u^-3+m*u), whose integral is uniformly bounded. Hence K(1-m)=-(1/2)ln m+O(1).
